prize_parts.citation: For experimental realisation of controllable strongly correlated quantum many-body systems with ultracold atoms in optical lattices, including the superfluid to Mott insulator transition, fermionic Hubbard physics and quantum gas microscopy

statement.case_for: I keep a single-part prize for ultracold atoms in optical lattices with the experimental trio. The core of the achievement is the demonstration that the Hubbard model can be built as a laboratory system with tunable parameters and read out quantitatively: the superfluid to Mott insulator transition, fermionic Hubbard physics and single-site-resolved quantum gas microscopy. These experiments have been reproduced by many independent groups for over twenty years, their interpretation is stable, and they changed how many-body statistical physics is done by giving access to regimes that analytic and numerical methods cannot reach. After reading the full exchange, my scientific judgment is unchanged and, if anything, firmer on maturity: it is the only shortlisted case where I see no open question about whether the central results are settled. I do not count the fact that B001 was named as an alternative by six members as evidence of merit; the case rests on the science. The chair asked whether any two-part configuration avoids rewarding the same laureates twice or exceeding three people per part. I do not see a good one: pairing B001 with B013 or B041 would need at least five distinct people and would break the three-person cap across the configuration, so a single part is the feasible output here.
statement.case_against: The credit cut from five names to three is the real weakness. An experiment-only trio leaves out Zoller and Cirac, whose proposals underlie the field, and Jaksch and Haensch are outside the credited list altogether, so the theory credit in the background material is incomplete however the citation is drafted. Priority among Bloch, Greiner and Esslinger on the first Mott and fermionic results is partly intertwined, and Esslinger's inclusion over Zoller is a judgment about whether the experiments or the proposal established the field. There is also the objection, which I take seriously, that analogue quantum simulation has so far reproduced known physics more than it has solved an open problem, and that a prize now rewards capability rather than a new result.

responses.point: Johansson moved to Bloch, Greiner and Zoller, arguing that a separate B011 theory prize is unlikely to be realised and that the lattice proposal is the origin of the discovery, while accepting that this makes the allocation more contestable than my trio.
responses.response: I understand the logic that B011 will not be prized separately, and I agree Zoller's proposal was decisive for the field. But that is an argument about what the final configuration can reach, not about what the experiments established. The Mott transition was an experimental observation, and the fermionic Hubbard realisation is Esslinger's own result. Dropping Esslinger to make room for Zoller would remove the one name that stands for the fermionic work, which is the part that links most directly to condensed-matter problems. A mixed trio with Zoller is a legitimate alternative citation, since the proposal is the origin, and I would not oppose it strongly if it was the committee's way of securing a majority. I still prefer the experiment-only trio because the citation is cleaner and the credit follows who demonstrated the physics. Theory credit would then be recorded in the scientific background, with Jaksch, Zoller and Cirac named there, rather than split across a prize.

responses.point: Eriksson holds that the prize-worthy part of magic-angle graphene is the flat-band prediction and the observed correlated states, and that an unsettled pairing mechanism is not the right bar for maturity.
responses.response: The distinction between existence and explanation is fair, and Eriksson and Olsson have persuaded me that the correlated insulators and superconductivity are robust and widely reproduced, so I now regard B041 as a strong alternative rather than a premature one. My remaining concern is different from the pairing mechanism. The credited trio omits first-author and device contributions that both of them admit cannot be repaired by the shortlist, and after only eight years the phase diagram is still being mapped, so a citation would have to describe a field in motion. I do not rank it first this year, but I would support it in a later year, and my objection is about readiness and credit, not about the quality of the result.

responses.point: Danielsson argues that for detector-driven discoveries the conception and construction of an instrument capable of finding a particle in huge backgrounds is the scientific contribution, and accepts that a 2:1 split between ATLAS and CMS follows from the three-person cap.
responses.response: I take this seriously, and the Higgs discovery is the greatest scientific weight on the shortlist. Danielsson's rule, honouring founding conception and construction, is coherent. The difficulty is that it is not applied the same way by Danielsson and Pearce, who choose Gianotti and Virdee respectively for the third name, and a rule that gives different laureates for two members using it in good faith is not yet a rule. Whichever of the two is picked, one collaboration is represented by a single person and the other by two, and the citation could not say who made the measurements. The Nobel statutes allow at most three, and I do not think the committee should settle on a configuration that it cannot defend to the physics community. I would reconsider only if the committee agreed on the principle first.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, notes that Mehlig and Pearce both exclude Zoller and Cirac from B001 and that the question of theory-experiment allocation matters, and asks whether a principled rule can be written for B020.
responses.response: On B001 the allocation question is real, and my answer is that the prize follows the experimental demonstrations, with the theorists acknowledged in the scientific background. On B020 I appreciate Pearce's candour about the instrumentalist bias and I agree that detector construction is real physics. But the same candour is a reason why the chair's own trio should not be used as the committee's rule. Virdee, Della Negra and Jenni cover construction, but then the person who led the experiment when the signal appeared is absent, and the committee cannot make this look neutral. I therefore treat B020 as unresolved on attribution, not as inferior science.

uncertainties: Whether the committee prefers the experiment-only trio (Esslinger) or a mixed trio with Zoller; I would accept either but think the experimental trio is the cleaner credit.
How the relative priority among Bloch, Greiner and Esslinger on the first Mott and fermionic Hubbard results will be judged.
Whether the committee judges quantum simulation to have produced new physics or mainly demonstrated capability.
Whether the attribution problem for B020 can be solved by a principle that both ATLAS and CMS supporters would accept.
Whether B041 will be seen as sufficiently mature this year.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile and nothing in the exchange changes that. I have not co-authored with any credited candidate for B001, B041, B013 or B020, and my own work on turbulence, stochastic processes and neural networks is distant from these fields, though statistical-mechanics interest in Hubbard-type models is a shared subject.
